spoilers.title: Romantic and sexual love
spoilers.html:
Briefly echoing back to the main point from the previous analysis that I made – about Selebus’ intentional “comparison and juxtaposition” approach in his writing – LiL is very, very consistent in how it treats romantic and sexual attraction as two sides of the same coin (for a whole bunch of self-evident reasons), which is why I am doing it here, as well, by including them as a pair rather than separately. There is the whole “porn” aspect of the game that explains why this is the case, sure, but the story *also* repeatedly poses complicated questions such as “how much overlap is there between the feelings of love and lust?” and “what happens when someone mistakes the former for the latter, or tries to substitute one for the other?”, which it explores mainly through Akira’s character (as this is pretty much the main crux of him as a person), as well as a few others, like post-awakening Sana.

On the other side of the spectrum, we have a similar exploration of how a fairly standard and natural development from “I like you” to “I love you” (and then to “I want to sleep with you”) – which is just how human attraction works, provided that all of the necessary conditions are fulfilled – can easily get twisted up in a million different and unpredictable ways, leading to a bunch of severe complications, confusion and emotional pain later down the line.

For example, perhaps you never wanted to be attracted to that person in the first place and would have been perfectly happy to just stay friends with them (or to just not interact with them at all), yet here we are, because emotions are stupid and the heart desires whoever the heart desires. Or maybe that person is already deeply in love with someone else, so you are now faced with a cruel dilemma of either having to selfishly compete for their love (against a person who potentially did literally nothing wrong) or resign yourself to being forever stuck with a painful one-sided yearning that is likely never going to be truly reciprocated. And that’s to say nothing of the unfortunate cases where the very things you feel are themselves considered utterly unacceptable by society at large – trying to come to terms with *that* is a whole different level of mental torment in and of itself.

Pretty much all of the girls in Lessons in Love fall under this umbrella of “I would probably be better off not having these feelings” in one way or another – some drastically more, some notably less – and can thus be broadly split into a few different categories based on the specifics of their situation (with a fairly frequent overlap between them, because the principle of “comparison and juxtaposition” *also* applies here, as well):

– The “self-destructive” group, for characters who slowly devolve into much worse versions of themselves, mentally and/or morally, the more they continue to feed their inner feelings without any regard for potential consequences: Chika, Sana, Makoto (kind of), Miku (also kind of), Ami, Otoha, Haruka and Sekai.

– The “inner conflict” group, for characters who are forced to decide between confronting a part of themselves they don’t like and indulging/changing it for the sake of further pursuing the newly-bloomed relationship, or staying exactly as they are right now, perfectly safe and familiar, too afraid to take a risk and thus likely dooming these feelings to never properly grow into anything: Yumi, Rin, Maya (both “Prime” and “Nu”, for their own different reasons), Molly, Tsuneyo (sort of, though her inner conflict is a bit different from the rest), Uta, Io, Otoha, Noriko, Kirin, Sara, Wakana/Osako (as a pair), Imani and Rika.

– The “explicitly taken advantage of” group, for the characters who possess some deep-rooted personal flaw or vulnerability and have been effectively coerced into their current predicament of being romantically/sexually involved with another person through their partner’s deliberate exploitation of those exact weaknesses: Futaba, Kaori (through Pareidolia’s/Sekai’s manipulation), Karin and Tsukasa.

(For the sake of clarification, the aforementioned list does *not* include the ubiquitous age/power disparity between Akira and everyone else in his class in the “taking advantage” category, because the entire narrative set-up of LiL makes this particular thematic point completely fucking moot due to the reasons that were very succinctly argued by Makoto in “T Is For Time (Trees & Threes)”.)

– The “love is blind” group, for the characters who would normally be amazing romantic partners, but suffer from falling for the worst person imaginable who has zero appreciation for what he has and treats them like shit: Chika (provided that you can stop her from going mental), Ayane, Makoto, Touka, Karin, Niki and Imani.

– The “love triangle” group, for the characters who are forced to compete with someone else for their chosen partner’s affection (once again, *not* counting the general disposition of everyone wanting to be with Sensei), or are themselves split between being attracted to multiple people: Chika, Rin, Maya (who not only has to contend with Akira’s other “true loves”, but with a past version of herself as well, if we’re talking about Nu Maya specifically), Molly, Uta and Io (in the context of the potential throuple), Otoha, Noriko/Niki, Haruka (in relation to her husband) and Wakana/Osako.

– The “forbidden attraction” group, for the characters whose feelings are commonly labeled as being extremely amoral and/or illegal: Ami, Nodoka, Otoha, Haruka, all three wizards (for obvious reasons) and Sekai.

– And, finally, the “lucky exceptions”: the characters who are either still mostly detached from this whole aspect of the narrative and are too busy dealing with their own separate things (Yasu, Yuki and *maybe* Tsuneyo, depending on how you interpret her current inner struggle), or, alternatively, *are* involved in a romantic/sexual relationship of some kind, but also have a full understanding of what their current arrangement actually entails and don’t really strive for more than what they already have (Miku, Maki and Tsubasa – although judging by Miku’s most recent events in 0.57, she might soon have to be moved from this category).

spoilers.title: Familial love
spoilers.html:
Now, looking back on the entire game thus far knowing all of what we do now, I think it’s fair to say that the theme of familial love (and the idea of “family” as a whole, with all of its positive and negative connotations) plays just as big of a role in Lessons in Love’s core overarching narrative as the similarly ever-pervasive aspects of sex and romance – which are, frankly, very much par for the course in a story belonging to the “adult” genre that also intentionally posits itself as a high-quality erotica.

This is something that, with the benefit of hindsight, naturally becomes much more obvious on a re-read, yet even a first-time reader – provided that they are observant enough and do not get deterred by the very overt incestual undertones of Ami’s character – will be able to pick up on many, many small details throughout the entirety of Chapter 1 that all ultimately link back to the subject of “family”: from Yumi’s, Ayane’s, Sana’s, Makoto’s and Tsuneyo’s stories all directly involving their parents in some way, to Chika’s and Chinami’s whole situation of being forced to take care of a younger sibling all on your own, to Sensei unconsciously and inadvertently embracing the role of Ami’s guardian (with her being the first girl he actually expresses genuine affection towards, rather than simply saying empty, insincere words in order to get them to spread their legs), etcetera – and it only gets more and more pronounced the longer the story goes on, with the introduction of the rest of the cast and various other family-related plot threads.

Family is *everywhere* in Lessons in Love, and no other character embodies this theme as prominently as Akira himself. Many people have already pointed out that him learning how to be a proper father figure (to *both* of his daughters) seems to be the main vector of personal growth for him at this present moment in the story, as despite Akira’s constant early remarks about how he “doesn’t want kids” and “hates the idea of being a parent”, his actions throughout all of Chapter 4 – and especially how he behaved during 0.53 with Himawari – clearly paint the complete opposite picture of his inner values. Not to mention the fact that Akira as a child *also* seemingly never had a proper father figure, having been raised entirely by a semi-abusive single mother (while the closest thing he had to a male role model in his entire life was somehow even fucking worse), so this subconscious desire of his to “be better than them” makes perfect sense on a thematical and narrative level, if we look at it from that angle.

Which, subsequently, brings me to the subject of the Arakawa family as a whole, and their individually unique and twisted perspectives on what it actually means to “love” your family members – something that seems to literally run in their blood at this point. Because, on one hand, we have Saki, who saw Akira less as her own son and more as an extension of Yuu (in addition to evidently carrying a lot of complicated religious baggage), and Nozomu, who absolutely fucking *despised* his younger brother to the point of treating him like a subhuman – yet, if Yasu in “Frankincense and Myrrh” is to be believed, both still somehow interpreted their actions as a “rough” form of love (like most abusers admittedly do). And on the other hand, we have Sekai, who despite being a genuinely good mother to Ami nonetheless had a whole slew of other equally worrying issues, most of which (like Sekai’s proclivity for incest or her inherent disregard for morals) she has managed to directly pass down to her daughter. Finally, from what little we do know of them, Yuu seemed to be an indecisive manwhore who couldn’t keep his dick in his pants, while Miu was apparently so bad that Sekai adamantly refused to ever respond to being called by her family name – clearly, there was no real love there, as well, or else this simply wouldn’t be the case.

Though even outside of the freak circus that is the Arakawa bloodline things are only really “better” in comparison – and quite marginally at that. Because for every Futaba, Uta, Otoha, Noriko and (arguably) Kirin: girls who come from unambiguously good, stable and loving families, with parents who care for their children and children who return said affection in kind – we have an overwhelming number of people like Chika (an orphan forced into a caretaker role at a very young age, having to look after a permanently sick sister), or Yumi (a self-raised child with a deadbeat addict mom), or Miku (another orphan with a life-long trauma), or Io (someone who would have been objectively better off *being* an orphan), or Nodoka (whose mother is a mindbroken vegetable), or Yasu (who lived through a very troubled childhood and then was promptly abandoned by her parents).

Hell, even among some of the better examples, who really is there? Ayane, with her absent mother and neglectful father? Makoto, who had to constantly deal with Maki being railed by random strangers downstairs (while Masahiro gleefully watched it all from his cuck chair), when the girl simply wanted to do her homework in peace? Molly, who lost her mother to suicide? Tsuneyo, whose dad is half-machine and already has one foot in the grave as is? Or the Tsukiokas, where the older daughter has the weight of the whole world put upon her shoulders, and the younger one is quite literally seen as disposable? At least Kaori and Nao-chan seem to be happy – good for them, genuinely.

Some of you might be wondering why I haven’t mentioned the Sakakibara family anywhere, and that is because the current relationship between Sana and Sara (and the way their dynamic has changed after the events of the second Nodokathon) is interesting enough to warrant talking about it in greater detail, especially with the new context from the most recent 0.57 update.

To be more precise, I no longer believe that Sana’s borderline sociopathic behavior and her insane disregard for Sara’s personal feelings is simply the result of the girl growing increasingly callous due to HOPE’s influence, as well as the unreserved indulgence in her newly developed hedonistic tendencies (which was my initial interpretation of the situation), and instead now lean towards the perspective of Sana being wholeheartedly motivated by a very twisted, yet seemingly sincere feeling of depraved familial love – making her much closer to Ami in this regard, rather than Nodoka.

So it’s not that Sana just fundamentally no longer cares about Sara to the point of being able to constantly guilt-trip her mother into doing whatever she wants without feeling even the slightest bit bad about it, but in fact the opposite: she *does* feel genuine affection towards Sara in her own incomprehensible way, and that is exactly *why* the girl is able to manipulate the woman with such a clear conscience – because in Sana’s mind, the end result of them living happily ever after together with Sensei as this sexually active semi-incestual family fully justifies whatever underhanded means she must use to get there, including repeatedly disregarding all of her mother’s personal boundaries and transforming their relationship into something that Sara actively doesn’t want.

Finally, before properly moving onto the next topic, I will briefly touch upon another less prevalent, but still very important form of familial love: love between siblings – because there is a surprisingly high variation of it in LiL, as well. Akira-Nozomu is the most obvious one (it’s a really cool detail that, even prior to the reveal in “Haiku”, *every single time* another character mentions loving their sibling “because we are family” or says something along the lines of “well, we are siblings, so we should always help each other”, you can immediately see Sensei starting to disassociate, usually accompanied by a brief meta-flash of a yellow smiling face), and, of course, there are the four main pair of siblings (Chika-Chinami, Touka-Tsukasa, Noriko-Niki and Kirin-Karin), all of whom have their own complicated relationship, where the girls’ affection towards each other is severely constrained by a different feeling: desperate need to pretend that everything is fine for the Chosokabes, overwhelming sense of filial duty for the Tsukiokas, having to deal with viewing your own sister as a romantic rival for the Nakayamas, and complete disconnect in their personal values (in addition to the major difference in how they are treated by both parents and peers alike) for the Kandas.

(Curiously, we *also* have a few “pseudo-sibling” bonds in the story, like Makoto-Miku, Futaba-Rin, Akira-Otoha, Akira-Noriko or Noriko-Ami – and, hell, throw in Akira-Nodoka in there too, just because of her “Perfect Hair Forever” – but I won’t be going into too much detail about them here, because this part is already way too fucking long as is.)

spoilers.title: Unconditional love
spoilers.html:
Like I already mentioned in my opening statement around three thousand words ago, the notion of “unconditional love” (or “agape”, as it is alternatively known) has two generally existing interpretations: the first one is the original Greek definition – the closest English equivalent of which is probably “soulmates” (though “soulmates” colloquially carries implicit romantic connotations, which was *not* necessarily how the Greeks used it) – while the second one is the later Christian adaptation of the same word, meaning “love of God for man and of man for God”. Unsurprisingly, LiL uses both, and each interpretation has its own unique applications within the bounds of the game’s expansive narrative canvas:

In regards to the former definition, we need to look no further than Sekai’s snide remark in “More Than Her”, where she mentions “[Akira’s] three true loves”: referring, of course, to herself, Niki and Maya. This is not just a throwaway line: upon closer inspection, there are indeed a few notable shared traits between these three characters – traits that are not individually unique to just them, but when put together *do* make them markedly stand out compared to all of the other people also pining for Akira’s heart. Specifically, all three have known Akira the longest, being there for him when he was living through some of his most formative life experiences; all three fully accept him as he truly is, despite his many-many flaws (this clearly doesn’t apply for Niki as strongly as it does for the other two, yet she does still accept Akira all the same, or else there would have been no possible reconciliation between them after the events of the “Mother Bonding trip”); and all three are also perfectly willing to follow the guy to the ends of the Earth without ever wavering from that chosen path, having their eyes on him and only him.

The *only* other girls who are *anywhere near* comparable to the aforementioned trio in terms of the sheer depth of their devotion – and, thus, the only other girls who are equally worthy of bearing the title of a “soulmate” – are, of course, the two remaining members of Sensei Love Squad: Ayane Amamiya and Ami Arakawa. Ami’s case is… weird, because while her love *is* “unconditional” in some sense of that word, there are nonetheless quite a lot of hidden stipulations that are tied to that “unconditionality” – stipulations that as of yet don’t have a clear explanation and, once broken, can easily make Ami do a complete 180 and instantly turn on Akira, despite still professing that she is “doing all of that for him”. Ayane’s love, however, has no such clauses, which is why she has been steadily rising in the rankings ever since Chapter 3 by repeatedly facing her fears and consistently proving the unmistakable strength of her feelings (plus, after the Aomori incident Ayane even fully fits the “being there for Akira when he was living through some of his most formative life experiences” criteria, so she has that going for her, as well). Between the two, I would definitely say that – as of right now – Ayane deserves the title of “Akira’s soulmate” way more than Ami does, though I sincerely hope that future revelations are going to level the field somewhat and make it a much more equal competition, because my shameless personal bias cannot tolerate seeing best girl Ami being shafted in such a way.

As for the latter definition of “agape”, this is where the whole “divine” aspect of the story comes into play, because despite LiL clearly presenting the Wishing Well pantheon as this weird materialistic corporatocracy that only cares about raw mutual benefits and has no space for any genuine spirituality, the specifics of how the God/human relationships work in this setting are *endlessly fascinating* to me, and I feel like there is a lot of nuance to them that doesn’t really get explored all that much.

In particular, there is a certain quote that Pareidolia says in “Friend” that has always stuck with me for whatever reason, and I continue coming back to it, because it completely recontextualizes the entire dynamic between “zillion-year-old deities” and “humans who have infiltrated their divine domain” into something almost “parent-child”-like:

“There are many ways in which one can become a God, but the part that *really* matters is being able to provide something for someone.

Look at cats and dogs and other domesticated animals – to them, humans are akin to God. They provide food, shelter, the whole shebang – and that’s what *we* do to *you*. Well, maybe not food or shelter: you guys have gotten pretty good at figuring that stuff out – but we give you something to believe in, and with how curious your species are that probably means… something?

I don’t know, man. There is a reason why we’re dying out, though – and it’s because you guys keep asking questions about how it’s even possible to be alive, when all logic states we shouldn’t. That shit’s annoying as hell, though, because most of us are *created* by you guys – so, like, why even bother creating a God at all when you’re just going to abandon it?”

Now, I might be talking out of my ass here (and if you think so, that’s okay – I kind of agree), but this entire passage reminds me a lot of the way many adults find meaning in life by becoming parents: they bring a new entity into the world – an entity that *needs* constant “worship”, or else it will die – and willingly pledge themselves to it, thus gaining a reason to persist in an otherwise aimless reality. And if what I’m describing here has any grain of truth to it, then it means that I half-lied earlier when I mentioned “two generally existing interpretations of unconditional love”, because that statement only referred to the notion of “agape” specifically, but “unconditional love” as a whole *also* has a third, much more commonly accepted definition: the love that a parent feels for their child, and vice-versa.

When looking at it from that perspective, a lot of other strange details in the setting suddenly start to make much more sense – like, for example, the fact that no matter how much Himawari tries to claim that “their co-existence is mostly symbiotic”, everything else that we know about the situation clearly indicates that it is *the Gods* who truly need humans to survive, not the other way around. A human can refuse to enter into a covenant with every single deity in existence and still presumably live their life like normal (Akira is a very fringe case and likely does not accurately reflect what being actively “sought out” by the divine normally looks like, yet even so he is still doing pretty alright, all things considered), but a God without any believers is inevitably going to get sent to eternally rest at the very bottom of the Wishing Well – I think that the true balance of power at play here speaks for itself. Similarly, a parent *can* always decide to neglect their child – or just simply never have one in the first place – and mostly be fine (outside of, like, potential social consequences, but those are whatever), whereas a child that gets neglected by their parents is probably going to be fucked for life, unless they can find someone else to fulfil that role.

Regardless of whether you agree with this reading or think that I’m spouting a bunch of nonsense, the end result surprisingly doesn’t change much even when viewed from a purely theological standpoint, as ultimately it all still comes back to love: our inherent need for acknowledgement and/or acceptance from others. Giving that love freely and unconditionally (by wholeheartedly putting your faith in a higher power, and then that higher power reciprocating said faith by fulfilling all that was promised and guiding you to a better future – *or* by nurturing a loving and supporting relationship with your child, taking care of them so that they later can take care of you) leads to a harmonious world full of kindness and prosperity, while withholding this love from those who desperately yearn for it (be it a believer rejecting the tenets of their deity, a God failing to fulfil its obligations towards the ones who worship it, a parent intentionally neglecting the well-being of their child, or a child responding to their parents’ care and affection with callous disregard) only leads to suffering, starvation and eventual destruction in the flames of hatred or despair.

Yet if we accept that everyone – both Gods and humans – *need* love to survive, and only through a mutual balance of give and take can the desired equilibrium be achieved, then what does it say about all of major deities we see in-game? Like HOPE, who only seems to take, but never give, treating his sole and most loyal disciple like a disposable pawn? Or Tenchou, who, on the contrary, only gives, but never takes, reducing himself to a dying, powerless husk? Or Pareidolia, who both gives *and* takes, but does it in a way where it is almost impossible to tell which is which? Likewise, the minor Gods are either too self-absorbed, caring for nothing but furthering their own agendas, or treat this whole thing like a boring job, barely engaging with their believers outside of simply fulfilling their part of the bargain, whereas the Xoanon just fundamentally appears to be above needing to be worshipped, concerning themselves only with their direct duties as the Librarian to the complete exclusion of everything and everyone else – more of a backstage machination given form, an observer that watches all and records all, than a “genuine” God in their own right.

If there is *any* Wishing Well-affiliated character who truly embodies the kabbalistic virtue of Chesed (“the kindness or love between people, and love or mercy of God towards humanity”) it would probably be Himawari, since her stated goal of creating HimawariCo: helping everyone achieve their own happy endings just because it’s the compassionate thing to do, with no strings attached – aligns most closely with the Christian definition of “agape”. Though she is also clearly out of her depth and is essentially fighting a losing battle against the status quo – which, in turn, does make me wonder whether the Wishing Well was “corrupted” somehow, leading to its current decaying corporatocracy state, of if the entire system was intentionally designed to be that way, because both the humans and the Gods that were created by them are just inherently flawed.

spoilers.title: Self-love
spoilers.html:
And, finally, there is the theme of self-love – not necessarily through the lens of narcissism (although there is quite a bit of that, too), but rather in the sense of “you cannot love others if you cannot love yourself first” – once again primarily exemplified through Akira, as well as a decent number of other characters with individual arcs related to personal growth, self-esteem, or any similar topics.

It’s a consistent narrative throughline that allowing yourself to be consumed by self-pity or hatred never leads to anything constructive and only serves to bring you even further down, preventing you from capitalizing on whichever unique strengths you *do* possess, which is why pretty much everyone who embodies this theme eventually reaches the point where they either decide to finally get their shit together or, alternatively, simply stop giving a fuck, embracing themselves in their entirety, flaws and all: Sensei getting a strong enough shock therapy to make him actually start doing shit for once rather than simply fucking around or wallowing in endless misery, Yumi learning how to let go of her delinquent persona and just generally turning her life around (which *also* applies to Yuki, as well), Miku slowly but surely getting comfortable with her own femininity, Futaba finally realizing just how much she has allowed herself to be used by Akira back in Chapter 1, Uta permitting herself to be genuine without needing to constantly hide behind a façade, Io (on Green Path exclusively) taking first bold steps towards reclaiming her sexuality, Otoha shooting her shot with Niki, Kirin entering her “good girl” arc, Haruka accepting that she is scum, Osako dealing with her feelings of inadequacy as a partner, Tsukasa rediscovering that she has worth as a person beyond her role as a “failsafe”, and Imani finding people she cares about and letting herself be vulnerable in front of them.

But, you're also wrong!

Prior to the 2023 reform, the prefectural specific laws you mention are referred to as the "prefectural youth protection laws". They did not include statutory rape level offense protection for youths, and were designed more as public-morality protections for minors rather than as full sexual-assault laws. Depending on which prefecture, most of them were less about consent, and more about inducing(Generally by paying, but did include other forms of coercion), sexual relations with someone under the age of 16-18. They also, of course, included laws about sexually explicit videos and pictures.

In most prefectures, if you were found in a sexual relationship with someone over the age of 13, but under the age of the local prefectural youth protection laws limit...the worst punishment was a fine of up to 3 million yen. In fact, most of the fines were less than 1 million yen. We're talking about less than $7k, at most $20k.

The most egregious cases(Imagine 13 year old and a 40+ year old), MIGHT see jail time, but even then it would have been 1 year or less.

The 2023 reformation raised the national level to 16, inline with a majority of the prefectural youth protection laws, but it also brought along with it all the actual consequences, such as statutory rape guidelines. Post 2023, Japan finally has real protections in place for those 13-17, and breaking them are tried at the federal level, which means real jail time and not pity fines.

Having said all of that I think Kumon-mi is outside of Tokyo, and Tokyo set the prefectural youth protection laws as 18, so Akira is liable to receive many fines for his various crimes of a sexual nature. He will also maybe lose his teaching license...It's also really sad that I need to say "maybe" cause it actually is a maybe. Japan wasn't exactly good about these things prior to 2023.
